5
The diameter of a circular disc is measured as (7.0  0.1) mm.
What is the area of the disc and the absolute uncertainty in the area?
area of disc
/ mm2
absolute
uncertainty / mm2

hints: Notice the measured quantity is diameter $d = (7.0 \pm 0.1) \text{ mm}$, so the fractional uncertainty in $d$ is $0.1/7.0$.
Recall the area in terms of diameter is $A = \pi d^2/4$, so $A$ depends on the second power of the measured $d$.
Double the fractional uncertainty to get that in the area, then multiply by the calculated area to get the absolute uncertainty and round to match the 2 significant figures of $7.0 \text{ mm}$.
walkthrough: Write the area using diameter: $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (d/2)^2 = \pi d^2/4$. Substitute $d = 7.0 \text{ mm}$ to get $A = \pi \times (7.0)^2/4 \approx 38.48 \text{ mm}^2$.
Find the fractional uncertainty in the diameter: $\Delta d/d = 0.1/7.0 \approx 0.0143$ or $1.43\%$.
Because $A$ is proportional to $d^2$, double the fractional uncertainty: $\Delta A/A = 2 \times \Delta d/d \approx 2 \times 0.0143 \approx 0.0286$ or $2.86\%$.
Convert to absolute uncertainty: $\Delta A \approx 0.0286 \times 38.48 \text{ mm}^2 \approx 1.1 \text{ mm}^2$, so $\Delta A \approx \pm 1 \text{ mm}^2$ to 1 significant figure.
Round the area to the same precision as the input with 2 significant figures: $38 \text{ mm}^2 \pm 1 \text{ mm}^2$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Gives $38.5 \text{ mm}^2 \pm 0.5 \text{ mm}^2$ but the $\pm 0.5$ uses only one times the fractional uncertainty in diameter, not doubled for $d^2$.

B.explanation: Gives $38 \text{ mm}^2 \pm 1 \text{ mm}^2$, which matches $A = \pi d^2/4$ with doubled fractional uncertainty and correct 2 significant figures.

C.explanation: Gives $154 \text{ mm}^2$ by using $\pi d^2$ instead of $\pi d^2/4$, treating the $7.0 \text{ mm}$ diameter as if it were the radius.

D.explanation: Gives $154 \text{ mm}^2$ by the same diameter-as-radius error, although its $\pm 4 \text{ mm}^2$ is the correctly doubled uncertainty for that wrong area.
